title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
An AI music generation system was trained on copyrighted recordings without authorization from the rights holders. The system was deployed and made available to users before these licensing agreements were reached, meaning it operated during a period when the rights to its training data were disputed. Catching this would have required either obtaining licenses before training the model or submitting the training dataset for rights clearance review before deployment.

The failure occurred in the model development stage, where copyrighted material was incorporated into training without the consent of Universal Music Group, Warner Music Group, Sony Music, or independent artists. A licensing review before deployment, or agreements negotiated before the system reached users, would have prevented the legal disputes that followed. It is not established whether rights holders were approached before deployment or whether the startup believed its use fell within legal boundaries.

Multiple lawsuits from different rights holders indicate the scope of the unauthorized training data. The settlement with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to build future platforms using only licensed music confirms the prior system relied on material the company did not have rights to use. Sony Music's separate lawsuits and independent artists' class action claims remain unresolved.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to end the dispute over copyrighted music used to train the company's artificial intelligence system. Udio creates original songs from text prompts using AI technology. The settlement includes Udio launching a new platform next year built only on authorized and licensed music, where users can customize, stream, and share their creations. UMG's CEO stated the agreements reflect their commitment to supporting artists and songwriters while embracing new technologies and business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, had been accused of using copyrighted hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to train its AI without permission or compensation. The startup declined to disclose financial settlement terms. Under the new agreement, artists can participate in the platform and receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. This marks Udio's first major music licensing deal. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
